subsection: 7. Economy and society: world crisis and from free trade to protectionism, 1922–1945

notes.h: The Free State's economic inheritance and the effects of partition
notes.b: The Free State inherited an economy dependent on exporting farm produce to Britain, and partition cut it off from the industrial north-east.
points: Agriculture dominated the Free State's economy: cattle, dairy products, bacon and eggs were exported mainly to Britain.
Partition separated the Free State from the industrial base of Belfast and the north-east, and the border interrupted trade in goods, labour and services.
The Free State had little heavy industry at independence, and the Belfast shipyards and linen mills remained in the north.
Many of the Free State's former British civil servants were retained, and the state's economic institutions were built on the Treaty settlement's financial terms.

notes.h: Cumann na nGaedheal's free trade and agriculture-led policy, 1922–1932
notes.b: The Cumann na nGaedheal governments believed that free trade and support for agriculture were the best route to prosperity, and they kept public spending low.
points: Patrick Hogan, Minister for Agriculture, promoted farming and the export trade, and the government supported dairying and cattle exports to Britain.
Ernest Blythe, Minister for Finance, followed fiscal conservatism; the 1924 budget cut old age pensions and reduced public spending.
The government avoided tariffs and industrial protection, and it treated free trade as the basis of the Free State's economy.
The Tariff Commission was set up in 1927 to consider applications for protection, and it recommended limited tariffs for some industries.
The Shannon Scheme, approved in 1925, was the government's main large-scale investment, and it gave the state its first major electricity supply.

notes.h: The world economic crisis and the depression, 1929–1933
notes.b: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 and the depression that followed reduced prices and demand for Irish exports, increased unemployment and deepened hardship in the cities.
points: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 began a worldwide depression that reduced trade and cut prices for Irish farm produce.
Unemployment and emigration rose in the 1930s, and the Free State's agricultural exporters faced falling incomes.
The depression exposed the weakness of an export economy that depended on a single large market, Britain, and made the case for protection stronger.
Fianna Fáil's arrival in power in 1932 coincided with the depression, and its response was to adopt protection rather than free trade.

notes.b: Fianna Fáil replaced free trade with protection, using tariffs, licensing and state investment to build Irish industry behind a wall of duties.
points: The Control of Manufactures Act of 1932 required Irish-owned control of some manufacturing businesses and restricted foreign investment in certain industries.
The Industrial Credit Company was set up in 1933 to lend to Irish industry, and its loans supported new manufacturing firms.
The Economic War increased the protection of Irish industry, with tariffs on British goods, and the government's industrial policy was built around import substitution.
Semi-state bodies, such as the Electricity Supply Board, were used to build state-owned services and to supply power.
The number of industrial workers in the Free State rose during the 1930s, but the growth was modest and depended on protection rather than on export markets.

notes.h: The Economic War and its costs for farmers
notes.b: The Economic War, from 1932 to 1938, hit cattle farmers hardest, as Britain's duties cut into the market that had sustained Irish agriculture.
points: British duties on Irish cattle and other farm exports fell hardest on cattle farmers, who had depended on live exports to Britain.
Irish farmers lost a large share of their traditional market, and the state's trade-war policies offered them only limited compensation.
The Economic War ended with the Anglo-Irish Trade Agreement of 1938, when duties on British and Irish goods were reduced.
The Economic War damaged the trade and incomes of the rural population, while helping to make the case for Irish industrial policy.

notes.b: Social policy in the Free State and Fianna Fáil's governments was limited, but it included housing, pensions and welfare measures that addressed the hardship of the depression.
points: The Free State's housing programmes in the 1920s and 1930s were limited, and many city families lived in tenements and overcrowded accommodation.
The Widows' and Orphans' Pensions Act of 1935 extended state support to widows and orphans, which was a significant but limited step.
Emigration remained high through the 1930s, and large numbers of young people left for Britain, the United States and other countries.
Unemployment remained high at the end of the 1930s, and the depression's effects on farm incomes lasted into the Second World War.

notes.b: McElligott was a senior civil servant whose influence on economic policy was exercised from inside the government. His impact is best understood through the Department of Finance's advice on protection and fiscal policy.
points: James J. McElligott was a civil servant in the Department of Finance and a leading adviser on economic and fiscal questions in the 1920s and 1930s.
He was part of the civil service network that advised ministers on tariffs, public spending and the financial terms of the Free State.
Contemporaries regarded the Department of Finance as a centre of caution, and McElligott was seen as a key influence on fiscal conservatism.
Historians have stressed the role of senior civil servants in shaping economic policy in the Free State, and McElligott is cited in this context.

notes.b: The Free State's economic performance was modest. Judgements depend on whether one measures the record by growth, by protection of industry, or by social welfare.
points: Achievement: Fianna Fáil's protectionism built some new industries and gave the state a measure of economic control through semi-state bodies.
Limit: industrial growth depended on tariffs and remained small, and the economy did not generate enough jobs to stop emigration.
Achievement: the Anglo-Irish Trade Agreement of 1938 ended the Economic War and settled the land annuities.
Limit: the Economic War cost cattle farmers heavily, and the state's welfare provision remained limited compared with Britain.
Contemporary view: supporters of protection argued that free trade had left the Free State dependent on Britain; critics argued that protection raised prices and limited exports.
Historians point to the difficulty of achieving economic success in a small, agricultural economy with a small domestic market and an emigrant population.

keyTerms.definition: A trade policy with no tariffs or barriers, which Cumann na nGaedheal governments favoured as the basis for the Free State's exports.
The use of tariffs, licences and state support to protect domestic industry from foreign competition, adopted by Fianna Fáil from 1932.
The body set up in 1927 to consider applications for tariffs and to recommend protection for industries.
The 1932 Act that restricted foreign ownership of some Irish manufacturing firms and supported Irish-owned industry.
The state-backed company set up in 1933 to lend to Irish industry and support the growth of new manufacturing firms.
The October 1929 collapse of the New York stock market, which began a worldwide depression that reduced demand for Irish exports.
State-owned companies, such as the Electricity Supply Board, set up to run key public services and industries.
A policy of replacing imported goods with goods made at home, behind protective tariffs.
The movement of people out of the country, which remained high in the Free State's economy through the 1930s.
The 1935 scheme that provided state pensions to widows and orphans, extending welfare beyond earlier provision.
